title: Nvidia takes Jensen Huang back as CEO, 11 days after he quit
subtitle: Nvidia's board voted unanimously on 23 Nov to reinstate its founder, while a probe goes on and new checks arrive.
content_html:
Picture a cricket team that drops its captain, and then, 11 days later, gives him the captaincy again. That is roughly what happened at Nvidia, one of the world's most valuable companies. On Monday, 23 November 2026, Nvidia's board voted unanimously to take Jensen Huang back as president, chief executive and board member, just 11 days after he resigned on 12 November.

First, who runs a company?

A big company is a bit like a school. The chief executive, or CEO, is the principal who runs things day to day. The chief financial officer, or CFO, looks after the money, like the person who keeps the fee register. Above them sits the board of directors, a small group that hires and fires the CEO for the owners of the company, its shareholders. Some board members are "independent": they do not work for the company, so they can judge it without fear or favour.

What happened on 12 November

On 12 November, Nvidia's board said Huang had resigned as president, CEO and board member, with immediate effect. Colette Kress, Nvidia's finance chief since September 2013, agreed to lead the company for the time being, while keeping her finance job. The board also named Harvey C. Jones as its first-ever chair, the person who leads board meetings, and began a search for a permanent new boss.

Why did he step down?

Nvidia has given one reason in its own words. Its 23 November statement points to "recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort". In simple words, news reports said a foreign spy agency had targeted him. That matter is still being investigated.

To check the matter, the board formed a committee made up only of independent directors, and that committee hired its own outside lawyers. Al Jazeera reports that US government investigations into the chipmaker are also under way.

Why the board changed its mind

According to Nvidia, the board held a series of talks and meetings with Huang. After them, the board felt satisfied with his honesty and his ability to lead. The board also received input from senior levels of the United States government, and on that basis it says it is confident his return brings no national security risk.

Board chair Harvey Jones said the board believes "Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA". Kress keeps her job as finance chief, and Jones stays on as chair. Huang ended his own statement with a short line: "I can't wait to get back to work."

The people who wanted him back

Huang's departure drew quick pushback in Silicon Valley, the part of California packed with tech companies. Within days, an online call for his return had drawn more than 1,80,000 signatures, Elon Musk among them, Al Jazeera reports. That count comes from the campaign itself.

Investors reacted too: Al Jazeera reports Nvidia shares jumped by more than 33 percent when US markets opened on Monday. This is not investment advice.

Who is Jensen Huang?

Huang was born in Taipei, Taiwan, in 1963 and moved to the United States as a child. In 1993 he co-founded Nvidia with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, launching it from a Denny's restaurant in San Jose, California.

Nvidia began by making graphics chips, called GPUs, for video games. A GPU is like a kitchen with hundreds of cooks, each chopping one small thing at the same moment, instead of one master chef doing everything. That same trick turned out to be perfect for training artificial intelligence. During the AI boom, Nvidia became the first company ever to be valued at more than $5 trillion, in October 2025, Wikipedia notes. In her 12 November statement, Kress spoke of "the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years".

He is back, but not fully in the clear

Coming back does not end the questions. Nvidia's 23 November statement lists three things that stay or change:

  • The probe goes on. The board says the independent committee's investigation "will proceed to conclusion". Huang fully supports it and has promised to cooperate.
  • A new watchdog group on the board. The board has formed a National Security and Export Control Committee, again made up only of independent directors. Rules called export controls are government rules on which goods, such as advanced chips, can be sold to which countries. This group keeps an eye on those trade rules and on national security risks.
  • A first-ever Chief Compliance Officer. Nvidia is searching for someone to fill this new role. Compliance means following the rules. Think of a referee inside the company, who checks that every team plays by the rule book and reports to a board committee.

Nvidia also says it will keep cooperating with ongoing government investigations and inquiries.

Rules, or trust in one founder?

Every company, from a samosa stall run by two friends to a giant chipmaker, faces the same puzzle. A founder often knows the business best, and staff, customers and investors may trust that person deeply. But a company also needs rules and checks that work no matter who sits in the top chair.

Nvidia's board did not pick just one. It brought back the founder. In the same statement, the board also added a new committee and a new rule-checking boss. For anyone dreaming of starting a company one day, that is a useful thing to notice: trust in a leader and a strong rule book can sit side by side.
